items.prompt: Match each change of state to what happens.
hints: Each change of state turns one state of matter into another.
Think of ice, water and water vapour, and which change turns one into the next.
Start with melting. Think about an ice lolly on a hot day.
items.explanation: Melting turns a solid into a liquid and freezing turns a liquid into a solid. Evaporating turns a liquid into a gas, and condensing turns a gas back into a liquid.

items.prompt: Sort these into solids, liquids and gases.
hints: Solids keep their shape, liquids flow and gases spread out to fill any space.
Some solids, such as sand, can be poured. Look at one grain to decide.
Start with the materials you cannot see, such as the air around you.
items.explanation: Ice, sand and wood are solids, and each grain of sand keeps its own shape even though sand can be poured. Honey, milk and oil are liquids, while water vapour, air and oxygen are gases.

items.prompt: The thermometer shows the temperature of some water. What state is the water in?

figure.alt: A thermometer showing minus 5 degrees Celsius.

options.text: solid ice
liquid water
options.why: Water is a liquid between 0 °C and 100 °C. This temperature is below 0 °C.

options.text: water vapour
options.why: Water vapour is a gas. At this temperature water is frozen, and it would need a lot of heat to become a gas.

options.text: boiling water
options.why: Water boils at 100 °C, not below 0 °C.

hints: Read the thermometer carefully. Check whether the temperature is above or below zero.
Pure water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.
Compare the reading with 0 °C first.
items.explanation: The thermometer shows minus 5 °C, which is below 0 °C, the temperature at which water freezes. So the water is solid ice.

items.prompt: Put these stages of the water cycle in order, starting with the sea.
items: the Sun heats water in the sea
rainwater flows in rivers back to the sea
hints: The water cycle is driven by heat from the Sun.
Water must become a gas before it can rise into the sky.
After the Sun heats the sea, think about what happens to the water at the surface.
items.explanation: The Sun heats the sea and water evaporates into water vapour. The vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds, then rain falls and rivers carry the water back to the sea.

items.prompt: Galih takes a glass of iced tea out of the fridge. Soon the outside of the glass is covered in drops of water. Where did the water come from?

options.text: The tea leaked through the glass.
options.why: Glass has no holes. The drops form even on a glass that holds only ice.

options.text: The glass started to melt.
options.why: Glass melts only at very high temperatures.

options.text: Water vapour in the air cooled and condensed on the cold glass.
The ice gave off water vapour that passed through the glass.
options.why: Nothing passes through the glass. The water comes from the air around it.

hints: The air around us contains water vapour that you cannot see.
Think about what happens to water vapour when it touches something cold.
Ask whether water could get through solid glass. If not, look outside the glass.
items.explanation: Air contains invisible water vapour. When it touches the cold glass, it cools and condenses into drops of liquid water.

items.prompt: A puddle on a concrete playground dries up on a sunny day. The water never reaches 100 °C. What happened to the water?

options.text: It went into the air as tiny drops of liquid.
options.why: In the air, the water is a gas called water vapour, not drops of liquid.

options.text: It evaporated. Evaporation can happen below the boiling point.
It froze.
options.why: It is a sunny day, so the water is warm, not frozen.

options.text: It disappeared and no longer exists.
options.why: The water still exists as water vapour in the air.

hints: Water does not have to boil to turn into a gas.
Think about how wet clothes dry on a line without ever boiling.
Cross out the choices that say the water froze or stopped existing.
items.explanation: The water evaporated. Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid at any temperature, and warmth from the Sun makes it faster.

items.prompt: Choose all the things that help wet clothes dry faster.

options.text: hanging them in the sun
hanging them where the wind blows
spreading them out
folding them into a pile
options.why: Folding hides most of the cloth from the air, so less water can evaporate.

options.text: keeping them in a closed cupboard
options.why: Air in a closed cupboard is still and cool, so evaporation is slow.

hints: Clothes dry when the water in them evaporates.
Think about what helps a puddle disappear quickly.
For each choice, ask whether more of the wet cloth is touching warm, moving air.
items.explanation: Sun, wind and spreading the clothes out all help water evaporate faster. Folding clothes or shutting them in a cupboard slows evaporation down.

items.prompt: Why is it often cooler and rainier on the high slopes of mountains in Java?

options.text: Mountains make rain from their rock.
options.why: Rock does not make rain. Rain comes from water vapour that cools and condenses.

options.text: The mountain top is much nearer the Sun.
options.why: A mountain is only a few kilometres high, which makes almost no difference to the distance to the Sun.

options.text: There is more sea water on mountains.
options.why: There is no sea on a mountain. The water comes from water vapour in the air.

options.text: Rising air cools, so its water vapour condenses into clouds and rain.

hints: Air gets colder the higher it goes.
Think about what happens to water vapour when it cools down.
Picture moist air from the sea being pushed up a mountainside. Follow it upwards.
items.explanation: Wind pushes moist air up the mountain, where the air is colder. The water vapour cools and condenses into clouds, which often bring rain.

items.prompt: A raindrop falls on a mountain in Java. Explain how the same water could end up in a cloud again. Use the words evaporate and condense.

criteria.label: Describes the water flowing or collecting, such as in a river or the sea
Explains that the Sun's heat makes the water evaporate
Explains water vapour rising, cooling and condensing into a cloud

planning: Where does the raindrop go after it lands?
What makes the water turn into a gas?
What happens to the gas high in the sky?
items.model: The raindrop runs down the mountain into a river, and the river carries it to the sea. The Sun heats the sea, and the water evaporates into water vapour. The water vapour rises and cools high in the sky. It condenses into tiny drops of water, which make a cloud.
hints: Follow the water downhill first.
Then think about what the Sun's heat does to water in rivers and the sea.
items.explanation: Water flows into rivers and the sea, then evaporates into water vapour when the Sun heats it. The vapour rises, cools and condenses into tiny drops that form clouds.

items.prompt: When a kettle boils, a white cloud appears a few centimetres above the spout. What is the white cloud?

options.text: water vapour, which is a white gas
options.why: Water vapour is invisible. You only see it after it condenses into tiny drops.

options.text: tiny drops of liquid water formed as water vapour cooled
smoke from the hot kettle
options.why: Nothing is burning. The cloud is made of water.

options.text: air that has turned white from the heat
options.why: Air does not turn white when it is heated.

hints: Look closely: there is a clear gap just above the spout before the cloud appears.
Water vapour is a gas that you cannot see.
Ask what happens to water vapour as it leaves the spout and meets cooler air.
items.explanation: Water vapour is invisible, which is why there is a clear gap at the spout. As the vapour meets cooler air, it condenses into tiny drops of liquid water that make the white cloud.

items.prompt: Label the parts of the water cycle.

figure.alt: A sea on the left, a mountain on the right, a sun in the corner and a cloud above the mountain slope. Arrows point up from the sea, rain falls from the cloud and a river runs down the mountain to the sea.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
Arrows pointing up from the sea show water rising as a gas.
Water falling from the cloud is the third stage.
items.explanation: Water evaporates from the sea, condenses into a cloud, falls as precipitation and runs back to the sea as run-off.

items.prompt: Tap the place where water vapour cools and turns into tiny drops of liquid water.

figure.alt: A sea on the left, a mountain on the right, a sun in the corner and a cloud above the mountain slope. Arrows point up from the sea, rain falls from the cloud and a river runs down the mountain to the sea.

hints: The change from gas to liquid is condensation.
Water vapour must cool before it condenses.
Look at the high, cold part of the sky.
items.explanation: Water vapour rises, cools and condenses into tiny drops. The drops gather to make a cloud.

items.prompt: Four identical puddles are set up. Tap the puddle that will dry up first.

figure.alt: Four boxes each hold an identical puddle. Top left: shade and still air. Top right: sun and still air. Bottom left: shade and wind. Bottom right: sun and wind.

hints: Warmth and moving air both speed up evaporation.
Look for the box that has both helpers.
Read the label in each box.
items.explanation: Heat and wind both make water evaporate faster. The puddle in the sun with wind has both.

items.prompt: Rani puts 40 ml of water in each dish for two days. Work out the water lost and complete the table.
head: Dish
Temp (°C)
Start (ml)
After 2 days (ml)
Water lost (ml)
hints: Water lost is the start amount take away the amount left.
Subtract for each row. Dish A is done for you.
Dish B: start at 40 ml and subtract 26 ml.
items.explanation: Dish B lost 40 - 26 = 14 ml and dish C lost 40 - 20 = 20 ml. Warmer dishes lost more water.

items.prompt: The bar chart shows the rainfall in a town. Which statement is supported by the data?

figure.alt: Bar chart of rain in cm each month: July 3, August 2, September 5, October 11, November 18, December 24.

options.text: July was the wettest month.
options.why: July was only 3 cm. Check which bar is tallest.

options.text: December had less rain than November.
options.why: Compare the two bars again. December is taller.

options.text: Rainfall rose every month from August to December.
Rainfall was the same in August and September.
options.why: August is 2 cm and September is 5 cm. They are different.

hints: Read the height of each bar carefully.
Compare each bar with the one before it.
Check August, September, October, November and December in turn.
items.explanation: The bars are 2, 5, 11, 18 and 24 cm from August to December, so each month is wetter than the last.

items.prompt: Use the bar chart. How many centimetres of rain fell in October, November and December together?

figure.alt: Bar chart of rain in cm each month: July 3, August 2, September 5, October 11, November 18, December 24.

hints: Read the three bars you need.
Add the three heights.
October is 11 cm. Add the next two bars to it.
items.explanation: 11 + 18 + 24 = 53 cm of rain in the three months.

items.prompt: Hadi heats a pan of water and records its temperature. What is happening to the water between 4 and 6 minutes?

head: Time (min)
Temperature (°C)
figure.alt: Table of water temperature while heated: 20, 40, 60, 80 at minutes 0 to 3, then 100 degrees Celsius at minutes 4, 5 and 6.

options.text: It is boiling and changing into water vapour at 100 °C.
Nothing is happening because the temperature stays the same.
options.why: The temperature stopped rising, but the water is still changing state.

options.text: It is freezing into ice.
options.why: Freezing happens when water cools, not when it is heated.

options.text: It is condensing into tiny drops.
options.why: Condensing is gas turning to liquid. The pan is being heated.

hints: Look at the temperature numbers from minute 4.
Water cannot get hotter than its boiling point as a liquid.
What state change happens to water at 100 °C?
items.explanation: At 100 °C the heat makes the liquid water boil and change into water vapour, so the temperature stays steady.

items.prompt: Put these events in order to show how water from a puddle could end up as rain.
items: Liquid water evaporates into water vapour.
The vapour condenses into tiny drops that make a cloud.
Drops join together and fall as rain.
hints: The Sun starts the whole process.
Think: warm, gas, cool, drops, fall.
The first step is the Sun warming the puddle.
items.explanation: Heat makes water evaporate. The vapour cools, condenses into a cloud and falls as rain.

items.prompt: Match each everyday event to the process that explains it.
pairs: Wet footprints vanish from hot paving
Hailstones fall from a storm cloud
Water flows from a river into the sea
hints: Decide if water is turning into gas, turning into liquid or moving.
The misted mirror is cold and meets warm, damp air.
Falling rain, snow and hail have a special name.
items.explanation: Drying is evaporation, misting is condensation, hail is precipitation and flowing water back to the sea is run-off.

items.prompt: Sort each event into evaporation or condensation.

items.text: A wet towel dries on a hot day
Drops form on a cold drink can
Dew appears on grass at dawn
A pond shrinks in the dry season
Windows mist up on a cold bus
Wet hair dries with a hairdryer

hints: Evaporation: liquid becomes gas. Condensation: gas becomes liquid.
Ask if water is leaving a surface or appearing on it.
Drying means water is going into the air.
items.explanation: Drying things lose liquid to the air by evaporation. Drops that appear on cool surfaces come from water vapour condensing.

items.prompt: When the Sun warms the sea, some water turns into an invisible gas called water ___.
hints: This gas is in the air around us.
You cannot see it, and it is not the white steam you can see.
It starts with the letter v.
items.explanation: The gas form of water is called water vapour. It is invisible.

items.prompt: Rain, snow, sleet and hail all fall from clouds. Together they are called ___.
hints: It is the word for water falling from the sky.
It is a stage in the water cycle.
It begins with the letter p.
items.explanation: Water that falls from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail is called precipitation.

items.prompt: Water vapour is a ___. High in the sky it cools and ___ into tiny drops. The drops make ___.
hints: Vapour means the gas form.
Gas to liquid has a special name.
Tiny drops high in the air gather together.
items.explanation: Water vapour is a gas. It condenses into tiny drops, and the drops make clouds.

items.prompt: Choose all the true statements.

options.text: Water vapour is a gas.
You can see water vapour in the air.
options.why: Water vapour is invisible. Mist and clouds are tiny drops of liquid.

options.text: Evaporation is faster in warm weather.
Condensation happens when air is heated.
options.why: Condensation happens when vapour is cooled.

options.text: There is water vapour in the air of a dry classroom.

hints: Check each statement on its own.
Mist you can see is made of liquid drops.
Water vapour is found in air everywhere, even if it feels dry.
items.explanation: Water vapour is an invisible gas that is in all air. Warmth speeds up evaporation, and cooling causes condensation.

items.prompt: What are clouds made of?

options.text: Water vapour only
options.why: Water vapour is an invisible gas. A cloud can be seen, so it must be something else.

options.text: Smoke from the ground
options.why: Clouds form from water, not smoke.

options.text: Steam from boiling seas
options.why: Seas do not boil. Water evaporates quietly from the surface.

options.text: Tiny drops of liquid water and ice crystals

hints: You can see clouds, so think about what can be seen.
Gas is invisible.
Clouds form after condensation.
items.explanation: When vapour condenses, it makes tiny liquid drops. High and cold, some freeze into ice crystals.

items.prompt: Maya seals a little water in a clear jar and leaves it in sunlight. Drops appear on the inside of the lid. Where did the water in the drops come from?

options.text: It leaked in through the lid from outside.
options.why: The jar is sealed, so no water can get in.

options.text: Water in the jar evaporated, then condensed on the cooler lid.
The glass made new water.
options.why: Glass does not make water. Water can only change state.

options.text: The lid is a solid, so it sweats.
options.why: A lid does not sweat. The drops came from the jar water.

hints: The jar is closed, so think about what is inside it.
Which change happens in sunlight, and which at the cooler lid?
Gas to liquid is the last step.
items.explanation: The sealed jar is a tiny water cycle. Water evaporates, then the vapour cools at the lid and condenses.

items.prompt: Yuki puts salty water in a bowl and covers it with clear plastic that slopes down to a small cup. She leaves it in the sun. Water collects in the cup. How does it taste?

options.text: Salty, because the salt evaporates with the water.
options.why: Salt is a solid that does not evaporate at this temperature.

options.text: Very salty, because the water became more concentrated.
options.why: The salt stays in the bowl, not in the cup.

options.text: Not salty, because only the water evaporates and the salt stays behind.
Sweet, because the Sun changes salt.
options.why: Sunlight does not change salt into something sweet.

hints: Think about which parts of the mixture can turn into a gas.
The water must evaporate, then condense under the plastic.
Where does the salt end up?
items.explanation: Water evaporates and condenses on the plastic, then drips into the cup. The salt is left in the bowl, so the water in the cup is fresh.

items.prompt: Sekar puts the same amount of water in a wide dish and a tall narrow cup in the same warm room. After two days, which has lost more water, and why?

options.text: The wide dish, because more of the water surface is open to the air.
The tall cup, because the water is higher up.
options.why: Height does not make water evaporate faster.

options.text: They lose the same, because the amounts of water were the same.
options.why: The surface area matters, not only the amount.

options.text: The tall cup, because it holds the water in a narrow space.
options.why: A narrow space slows evaporation.

hints: Evaporation happens at the surface of the water.
Compare how much surface each container shows to the air.
A bigger surface lets more water escape.
items.explanation: Evaporation happens at the surface, so the wide dish with more surface area loses water faster.

items.prompt: Dewi sees small drops of water on the grass early in the morning. Where did the water come from?

options.text: The grass made the water inside its leaves.
options.why: Dew forms outside the leaf from water in the air.

options.text: Water vapour in the air cooled at night and condensed on the cold grass.
It rained very lightly in the night.
options.why: Dew is not rain. It forms on cold surfaces from vapour in the air.

options.text: The soil evaporated the water straight onto the leaves.
options.why: Dew gathers on the surface it forms on, from the air.

hints: Cold surfaces cool the air that touches them.
Which change takes a gas to a liquid?
Think of drops on a cold glass.
items.explanation: The cold grass cools the air touching it, so water vapour condenses into drops of dew.
